learn.intro: The 'Second Cold War' of the early 1980s brought Afghanistan, new missiles in Europe, Solidarity and Reagan's SDI. Then Gorbachev, facing a failing economy, transformed relations: summits, the INF Treaty, the end of Soviet control in Eastern Europe and German reunification in 1990.

blocks.p: Soviet leadership: Brezhnev died in November 1982; Andropov (1982–84) and Chernenko (1984–85) were old and ill. Gromyko remained Foreign Minister until 1985. Gorbachev became leader in March 1985 and, with Foreign Minister Shevardnadze, pursued 'new thinking' in foreign policy.

Western leaders: Reagan (President 1981–89) called the USSR an 'evil empire' (1983) and built up US forces, but later negotiated with Gorbachev. Thatcher was a close ally of Reagan who said after meeting Gorbachev (December 1984) that he was someone the West could do business with. Pope John Paul II (elected 1978), a Pole, visited Poland in 1979 and inspired opposition to communism. Deng Xiaoping led China from the late 1970s, opening its economy and improving relations with the USA (formal diplomatic relations, 1979).

Summits: Geneva (November 1985) built personal trust; Reykjavik (October 1986) nearly agreed to abolish nuclear weapons but broke down over SDI; Washington (December 1987) signed the INF Treaty; Moscow (1988); Malta (December 1989), often described as marking the end of the Cold War.

sections.title: 2. Heightened tensions in the early 1980s

blocks.p: Afghanistan: the USSR invaded in December 1979 to prop up a communist government. The USA responded with the Carter Doctrine, a grain embargo and a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics, and supplied the mujahideen. The war became costly for the USSR.

New missiles in Europe: Soviet SS-20 missiles led NATO to its 'dual-track' decision (December 1979) to deploy US Pershing II and cruise missiles while negotiating. Deployment from late 1983 caused mass peace protests in Western Europe. The shooting down of the airliner KAL 007 (September 1983) and the NATO exercise Able Archer (November 1983) raised tension further.

Solidarity: the independent trade union led by Lech Wałęsa grew out of the Gdańsk strikes (August 1980). Martial law was declared in Poland in December 1981. Solidarity's survival underground showed the weakness of communist legitimacy.

Reagan and SDI: Reagan increased defence spending and in March 1983 announced the Strategic Defense Initiative ('Star Wars'), a space-based missile shield. Moscow feared it could neither match it technologically nor afford to try.

evidence: December 1979: Afghanistan invaded; NATO dual-track decision.

sections.title: 3. The economics of the Cold War in the 1980s

blocks.p: US technology and spending: computer and electronics advances underpinned precision weapons and SDI research; a large defence build-up was funded by borrowing.

Soviet economic problems: stagnation under Brezhnev, inefficient central planning, falling productivity, the cost of the arms race and of Afghanistan, and subsidies to allies. The collapse in world oil prices (1986) cut export earnings; the Chernobyl disaster (April 1986) exposed technological and political failings. Gorbachev's reforms — perestroika (economic restructuring) and glasnost (openness) — needed lower military spending and better relations with the West.

sections.title: 4. The breakdown of the USSR and Soviet control of Eastern Europe

blocks.p: Gorbachev abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine: Eastern European states could choose their own path (sometimes called the 'Sinatra Doctrine'). Soviet troops completed withdrawal from Afghanistan in February 1989.

1989 in Eastern Europe: Hungary began dismantling its border fence with Austria (from May 1989), opening an escape route; Poland held partly free elections (June 1989) and Solidarity won; the Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989; Czechoslovakia's 'Velvet Revolution' (November–December 1989) ended communist rule.

Nationalism inside the USSR: Soviet troops killed protesters in Tbilisi, Georgia (April 1989); the Baltic states organised the 'Baltic Way' human chain (August 1989) and Lithuania declared independence in March 1990.

German reunification: after free elections in East Germany (March 1990) and the Two Plus Four Treaty (September 1990), Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990 inside NATO — a decisive sign that the Cold War division of Europe was over.

misconceptions.wrong: Glasnost and perestroika mean the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Glasnost = openness; perestroika = restructuring. Examiners report frequent confusion.

evidence.model: The cost of the arms race and Afghanistan, stagnation, the 1986 oil price collapse and the Chernobyl disaster (April 1986).

flashcards.q: Why did tension rise in the early 1980s?
flashcards.a: Afghanistan, SS-20s vs Pershing II/cruise, Solidarity and martial law, Reagan's rhetoric and SDI, KAL 007, Able Archer.

flashcards.q: Why were the summits of 1985–89 significant?
flashcards.a: Built trust (Geneva), nearly abolished weapons (Reykjavik), INF Treaty (Washington), end of Cold War (Malta).

flashcards.q: How did economics help end the Cold War?
flashcards.a: The USSR could not afford the arms race or match US technology; Gorbachev needed lower military spending for reform.
flashcards.hint: Link to the ending, not just collapse.

flashcards.q: Key events of 1989 in Eastern Europe?
flashcards.a: Hungary opens border; Polish elections; Berlin Wall opened; Velvet Revolution.

flashcards.q: Why did German reunification matter for superpower relations?
flashcards.a: It ended the division of Europe; a united Germany stayed in NATO with Soviet agreement.

I can explain the causes of heightened tension in the early 1980s.
I can judge the significance of economics in ending the Cold War.
I can describe the breakdown of Soviet control in Eastern Europe and German reunification.

questions.label: Past paper: WHI04/1C, January 2025, Q3
questions.q: How far do you agree that, in the years 1985–90, the most significant factor in bringing the Cold War to an end was the impact of economic problems within the USSR?

model.t: Economic problems within the USSR were a crucial factor in ending the Cold War in 1985–90 because they forced Gorbachev to reduce the cost of confrontation. However, Gorbachev's 'new thinking', Reagan's willingness to negotiate and the collapse of communist rule in Eastern Europe also explain how it ended. Judged by impact, economic problems were the most significant underlying factor, but Gorbachev's choices turned them into an ending.
model.n: Introduction: focuses on HOW the Cold War ended (examiners warn against explaining only why the USSR collapsed), names alternatives and criteria.

model.t: Point: Soviet economic weakness had a fundamental impact because the USSR could no longer afford the arms race.
model.n: P — links the factor to a criterion (impact).

model.t: Evidence: by the mid-1980s the economy was stagnating; the war in Afghanistan was costly; the fall in world oil prices in 1986 cut export earnings; and Chernobyl (April 1986) exposed technological failings while the USA was investing in SDI.
model.n: E — precise, accurate and dated (watch the chronology — Gorbachev only from March 1985).

model.t: Explain: as a result Gorbachev needed to cut military spending to fund perestroika, which led him to seek arms reductions such as the INF Treaty (1987) and to withdraw from Afghanistan (completed February 1989).
model.n: E — explicitly connects economics to the ENDING of the Cold War.

model.t: Judge: however, economic problems alone did not decide the outcome — earlier leaders faced stagnation without ending the Cold War — so their significance depended on Gorbachev's decision to abandon the Brezhnev Doctrine.
model.n: J — weighs the factor against another, using a valid comparison.

model.t: Conclusion: Overall, economic problems were the most significant factor in terms of impact and duration because they created the pressure for change, but they ended the Cold War only in combination with Gorbachev's new thinking and the events of 1989–90.
model.n: Conclusion: ranked judgement using criteria; avoids just listing factors.

questions.model_note: Illustrative model written for this site (introduction, one PEEJ paragraph and conclusion), following the department factor frame and the January 2025 examiner advice. It is not a Pearson exemplar.
